title: Striking Back at Lightning With Lasers

paragraphs: Seldom is the weather more dramatic than when thunderstorms strike. Their electrical fury inflicts death or serious injury on around 500 people each year in the United States alone. As the clouds roll in, a leisurely round of golf can become a terrifying dice with death – out in the open, a lone golfer may be a lightning bolt’s most inviting target. And there is damage to property too. Lightning damage costs American power companies more than $100 million a year.

But researchers in the United States and Japan are planning to hit back. Already in laboratory trials they have tested strategies for neutralising the power of thunderstorms, and this winter they will brave real storms, equipped with an armoury of lasers that they will be pointing towards the heavens to discharge thunderclouds before lightning can strike.

The idea of forcing storm clouds to discharge their lightning on command is not new. In the early 1960s, researchers tried firing rockets trailing wires into thunderclouds to set up an easy discharge path for the huge electric charges that these clouds generate. The technique survives to this day at a test site in Florida run by the University of Florida, with support from the Electrical Power Research Institute (EPRI), based in California. EPRI, which is funded by power companies, is looking at ways to protect the United States’ power grid from lightning strikes. ‘We can cause the lightning to strike where we want it to using rockets,’ says Ralph Bernstein, manager of lightning projects at EPRI. The rocket site is providing precise measurements of lightning voltages and allowing engineers to check how electrical equipment bears up.

sections.label: Bad behaviour
paragraphs: But while rockets are fine for research, they cannot provide the protection from lightning strikes that everyone is looking for. The rockets cost around $1,200 each, can only be fired at a limited frequency and their failure rate is about 40 per cent. And even when they do trigger lightning, things still do not always go according to plan. ‘Lightning is not perfectly well behaved,’ says Bernstein. ‘Occasionally, it will take a branch and go someplace it wasn’t supposed to go.’

And anyway, who would want to fire streams of rockets in a populated area? ‘What goes up must come down,’ points out Jean-Claude Diels of the University of New Mexico. Diels is leading a project, which is backed by EPRI, to try to use lasers to discharge lightning safely – and safety is a basic requirement since no one wants to put themselves or their expensive equipment at risk. With around $500,000 invested so far, a promising system is just emerging from the laboratory.

The idea began some 20 years ago, when high-powered lasers were revealing their ability to extract electrons out of atoms and create ions. If a laser could generate a line of ionisation in the air all the way up to a storm cloud, this conducting path could be used to guide lightning to Earth, before the electric field becomes strong enough to break down the air in an uncontrollable surge. To stop the laser itself being struck, it would not be pointed straight at the clouds. Instead it would be directed at a mirror, and from there into the sky. The mirror would be protected by placing lightning conductors close by. Ideally, the cloud-zapper (gun) would be cheap enough to be installed around all key power installations, and portable enough to be taken to international sporting events to beam up at brewing storm clouds.

sections.label: A stumbling block
paragraphs: However, there is still a big stumbling block. The laser is no nifty portable: it’s a monster that takes up a whole room. Diels is trying to cut down the size and says that a laser around the size of a small table is in the offing. He plans to test this more manageable system on live thunderclouds next summer.

Bernstein says that Diels’s system is attracting lots of interest from the power companies. But they have not yet come up with the $5 million that EPRI says will be needed to develop a commercial system, by making the lasers yet smaller and cheaper. ‘I cannot say I have money yet, but I’m working on it,’ says Bernstein. He reckons that the forthcoming field tests will be the turning point – and he’s hoping for good news. Bernstein predicts ‘an avalanche of interest and support’ if all goes well. He expects to see cloud-zappers eventually costing $50,000 to $100,000 each.

Other scientists could also benefit. With a lightning ‘switch’ at their fingertips, materials scientists could find out what happens when mighty currents meet matter. Diels also hopes to see the birth of ‘interactive meteorology’ – not just forecasting the weather but controlling it. ‘If we could discharge clouds, we might affect the weather,’ he says.

And perhaps, says Diels, we’ll be able to confront some other meteorological menaces. ‘We think we could prevent hail by inducing lightning,’ he says. Thunder, the shock wave that comes from a lightning flash, is thought to be the trigger for the torrential rain that is typical of storms. A laser thunder factory could shake the moisture out of clouds, perhaps preventing the formation of the giant hailstones that threaten crops. With luck, as the storm clouds gather this winter, laser-toting researchers could, for the first time, strike back.

answerEvidence.evidence: Striking Back at Lightning With Lasers
answerEvidence.reason: The title states the article’s controlling subject, and the body develops the laser method, its mechanism, limitations, funding and proposed uses.

distractors.A: Golf appears only as an opening example of personal danger; the article does not discuss damage to golf courses as its main subject.
distractors.B: Power-grid protection is one motivation, but the article does not compare effects on US and Japanese power supplies.
distractors.C: The rocket method supplies background and contrast; the sustained focus is the laser technique, not a survey of many control methods.

answerEvidence.evidence: And there is damage to property too. Lightning damage costs American power companies more than $100 million a year.
answerEvidence.reason: The passage explicitly describes major annual property damage and quantifies the cost to American power companies.

distractors.B: A golfer is used as one vivid example; the passage says around 500 people, not mainly golfers, are killed or seriously injured.
distractors.C: The figure of around 500 applies to the United States alone, not the whole world.
distractors.D: The text gives a monetary loss of more than $100 million, not a count of more than 100 companies.

answerEvidence.evidence: The technique survives to this day at a test site in Florida run by the University of Florida, with support from the Electrical Power Research Institute (EPRI), based in California.
answerEvidence.corroboratingEvidence: Diels is leading a project, which is backed by EPRI, to try to use lasers to discharge lightning safely – and safety is a basic requirement since no one wants to put themselves or their expensive equipment at risk.
answerEvidence.reason: Both university projects receive support from EPRI, so they share the same funding source.

distractors.B: Florida uses rockets trailing wires, whereas New Mexico is developing a laser system.
distractors.C: The researchers are university-based; commercial power companies fund EPRI but do not employ both research groups.
distractors.D: The projects pursue related protective aims and share EPRI support; no opposition is stated.

answerEvidence.evidence: EPRI, which is funded by power companies, is looking at ways to protect the United States’ power grid from lightning strikes.
answerEvidence.reason: The exact source words completing ‘financial support from’ are ‘power companies’ and satisfy the two-word limit.

answerEvidence.evidence: Diels is leading a project, which is backed by EPRI, to try to use lasers to discharge lightning safely – and safety is a basic requirement since no one wants to put themselves or their expensive equipment at risk.
answerEvidence.reason: The adverb ‘safely’ states the technique’s advantage and grammatically completes ‘can be used safely’.

answerEvidence.evidence: The laser is no nifty portable: it’s a monster that takes up a whole room. Diels is trying to cut down the size and says that a laser around the size of a small table is in the offing.
answerEvidence.reason: The obstacle is the equipment’s room-filling size, and ‘size’ directly completes the possessive phrase ‘its size’.

answerEvidence.evidence: The idea began some 20 years ago, when high-powered lasers were revealing their ability to extract electrons out of atoms and create ions.
answerEvidence.reason: The passage directly states that electrons are extracted from atoms; option B is ‘atoms’.

distractors.A: Cloud-zappers are the proposed laser devices, not matter from which electrons are removed.
distractors.C: Storm clouds are the distant target reached by the ionised path, not the source of the extracted electrons.
distractors.D: Mirrors redirect the beam; electrons are not removed from them.
distractors.E: ‘Technique’ is an abstract method and cannot supply atoms whose electrons are extracted.
distractors.F: Ions are created after electrons are removed from atoms; they are the result, not the source.
distractors.G: Rockets belong to the older triggering method and are not ionised by this laser description.
distractors.H: Conductors protect the mirror; the passage does not say the laser removes electrons from them.
distractors.I: Thunder is a shock wave discussed later and is not the material being ionised.

answerEvidence.evidence: If a laser could generate a line of ionisation in the air all the way up to a storm cloud, this conducting path could be used to guide lightning to Earth, before the electric field becomes strong enough to break down the air in an uncontrollable surge.
answerEvidence.reason: The ionised path extends to a storm cloud so that its electrical charge can be discharged; option C is ‘storm clouds’.

distractors.A: A cloud-zapper is the laser apparatus itself, not the target at which the laser is directed.
distractors.B: Atoms are the source of electrons in the ionisation process, not the atmospheric target.
distractors.D: The beam is aimed at a mirror first for protection, but the method’s electrical target is the storm cloud; mirrors answer Q10.
distractors.E: A technique is not a physical target for a laser beam.
distractors.F: Ions are created in the air and form the conducting path; the beam is not described as being directed at ions.
distractors.G: Rockets are the older alternative method, not the laser’s target.
distractors.H: Lightning conductors are placed near the mirror for protection, not targeted to control cloud charges.
distractors.I: Thunder is a sound shock wave and is not where the laser is directed.

answerEvidence.evidence: And anyway, who would want to fire streams of rockets in a populated area? ‘What goes up must come down,’ points out Jean-Claude Diels of the University of New Mexico. Diels is leading a project, which is backed by EPRI, to try to use lasers to discharge lightning safely – and safety is a basic requirement since no one wants to put themselves or their expensive equipment at risk.
answerEvidence.reason: The text contrasts hazardous streams of rockets with Diels’s aim of discharging lightning safely; option G is ‘rockets’.

distractors.A: Cloud-zappers are the laser devices being developed, so they are not the older, more dangerous comparison method.
distractors.B: Atoms are involved in ionisation, not used as a competing lightning-control method.
distractors.C: Storm clouds are acted upon; they are not a method that people ‘use’.
distractors.D: Mirrors are a protective component of the laser setup, not the dangerous alternative.
distractors.E: ‘Technique’ is too generic and does not identify the explicitly criticised method.
distractors.F: Ions form the conducting path and are not a separate control technology.
distractors.H: Conductors protect the mirror and are not presented as dangerous.
distractors.I: Thunder is a natural shock wave, not a method used to control electrical charges.

answerEvidence.evidence: To stop the laser itself being struck, it would not be pointed straight at the clouds. Instead it would be directed at a mirror, and from there into the sky.
answerEvidence.reason: The beam is aimed first at a mirror to protect the laser; option D is ‘mirrors’.

distractors.A: Cloud-zappers are the laser systems being protected, not the first object struck by their beams.
distractors.B: Atoms lose electrons during ionisation, but they are not named as the first aiming point.
distractors.C: The beam ultimately goes towards storm clouds, but it is deliberately not pointed straight at them; ‘firstly’ requires mirrors.
distractors.E: A technique cannot serve as a physical aiming point.
distractors.F: Ions are produced by the beam and are not the first target.
distractors.G: Rockets belong to a different method and do not redirect the laser beam.
distractors.H: Conductors are placed close to the mirror to protect it; the beam is not aimed at them.
distractors.I: Thunder is a sound effect and cannot redirect or protect the laser.

answerEvidence.evidence: But they have not yet come up with the $5 million that EPRI says will be needed to develop a commercial system, by making the lasers yet smaller and cheaper.
answerEvidence.reason: The statement says enough development money has been provided, whereas the passage explicitly says the required $5 million has not yet been found.

distractors.YES: This reverses the passage’s explicit ‘have not yet come up with’ statement.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The funding shortfall is directly stated, so the claim is decidably false rather than absent.

answerEvidence.evidence: He reckons that the forthcoming field tests will be the turning point – and he’s hoping for good news. Bernstein predicts ‘an avalanche of interest and support’ if all goes well.
answerEvidence.reason: Future support is conditional on successful forthcoming field tests, matching the statement that funding will depend on tests in real storms.

distractors.NO: The passage supports rather than contradicts the dependency: support is predicted only ‘if all goes well’ in the field tests.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The connection between field-test success and subsequent support is explicitly stated.

answerEvidence.evidence: Diels also hopes to see the birth of ‘interactive meteorology’ – not just forecasting the weather but controlling it.
answerEvidence.reason: The passage discusses Diels’s hope for interactive meteorology but never states whether weather forecasters are interested, intensely or otherwise, in his system.

distractors.YES: No sentence attributes intense interest to weather forecasters; the explicit interested group is power companies.
distractors.NO: The passage also does not state that weather forecasters lack interest, so the claim is not contradicted.

bodyParagraphs: Seldom is the weather more dramatic than when thunderstorms strike. Their electrical fury inflicts death or serious injury on around 500 people each year in the United States alone. As the clouds roll in, a leisurely round of golf can become a terrifying dice with death – out in the open, a lone golfer may be a lightning bolt’s most inviting target. And there is damage to property too. Lightning damage costs American power companies more than $100 million a year.

But researchers in the United States and Japan are planning to hit back. Already in laboratory trials they have tested strategies for neutralising the power of thunderstorms, and this winter they will brave real storms, equipped with an armoury of lasers that they will be pointing towards the heavens to discharge thunderclouds before lightning can strike.

The idea of forcing storm clouds to discharge their lightning on command is not new. In the early 1960s, researchers tried firing rockets trailing wires into thunderclouds to set up an easy discharge path for the huge electric charges that these clouds generate. The technique survives to this day at a test site in Florida run by the University of Florida, with support from the Electrical Power Research Institute (EPRI), based in California. EPRI, which is funded by power companies, is looking at ways to protect the United States’ power grid from lightning strikes. ‘We can cause the lightning to strike where we want it to using rockets,’ says Ralph Bernstein, manager of lightning projects at EPRI. The rocket site is providing precise measurements of lightning voltages and allowing engineers to check how electrical equipment bears up.

But while rockets are fine for research, they cannot provide the protection from lightning strikes that everyone is looking for. The rockets cost around $1,200 each, can only be fired at a limited frequency and their failure rate is about 40 per cent. And even when they do trigger lightning, things still do not always go according to plan. ‘Lightning is not perfectly well behaved,’ says Bernstein. ‘Occasionally, it will take a branch and go someplace it wasn’t supposed to go.’

And anyway, who would want to fire streams of rockets in a populated area? ‘What goes up must come down,’ points out Jean-Claude Diels of the University of New Mexico. Diels is leading a project, which is backed by EPRI, to try to use lasers to discharge lightning safely – and safety is a basic requirement since no one wants to put themselves or their expensive equipment at risk. With around $500,000 invested so far, a promising system is just emerging from the laboratory.

The idea began some 20 years ago, when high-powered lasers were revealing their ability to extract electrons out of atoms and create ions. If a laser could generate a line of ionisation in the air all the way up to a storm cloud, this conducting path could be used to guide lightning to Earth, before the electric field becomes strong enough to break down the air in an uncontrollable surge. To stop the laser itself being struck, it would not be pointed straight at the clouds. Instead it would be directed at a mirror, and from there into the sky. The mirror would be protected by placing lightning conductors close by. Ideally, the cloud-zapper (gun) would be cheap enough to be installed around all key power installations, and portable enough to be taken to international sporting events to beam up at brewing storm clouds.

However, there is still a big stumbling block. The laser is no nifty portable: it’s a monster that takes up a whole room. Diels is trying to cut down the size and says that a laser around the size of a small table is in the offing. He plans to test this more manageable system on live thunderclouds next summer.

Bernstein says that Diels’s system is attracting lots of interest from the power companies. But they have not yet come up with the $5 million that EPRI says will be needed to develop a commercial system, by making the lasers yet smaller and cheaper. ‘I cannot say I have money yet, but I’m working on it,’ says Bernstein. He reckons that the forthcoming field tests will be the turning point – and he’s hoping for good news. Bernstein predicts ‘an avalanche of interest and support’ if all goes well. He expects to see cloud-zappers eventually costing $50,000 to $100,000 each.

Other scientists could also benefit. With a lightning ‘switch’ at their fingertips, materials scientists could find out what happens when mighty currents meet matter. Diels also hopes to see the birth of ‘interactive meteorology’ – not just forecasting the weather but controlling it. ‘If we could discharge clouds, we might affect the weather,’ he says.

And perhaps, says Diels, we’ll be able to confront some other meteorological menaces. ‘We think we could prevent hail by inducing lightning,’ he says. Thunder, the shock wave that comes from a lightning flash, is thought to be the trigger for the torrential rain that is typical of storms. A laser thunder factory could shake the moisture out of clouds, perhaps preventing the formation of the giant hailstones that threaten crops. With luck, as the storm clouds gather this winter, laser-toting researchers could, for the first time, strike back.

Questions 1–3
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 1–3 on your answer sheet.
1 The main topic discussed in the text is
A the damage caused to US golf courses and golf players by lightning strikes.
B the effect of lightning on power supplies in the US and in Japan.
C a variety of methods used in trying to control lightning strikes.
D a laser technique used in trying to control lightning strikes.
2 According to the text, every year lightning
A does considerable damage to buildings during thunderstorms.
B kills or injures mainly golfers in the United States.
C kills or injures around 500 people throughout the world.
D damages more than 100 American power companies.
3 Researchers at the University of Florida and at the University of New Mexico
A receive funds from the same source.
B are using the same techniques.
C are employed by commercial companies.
D are in opposition to each other.
Questions 4–6
Complete the sentences below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 4–6 on your answer sheet.
4 EPRI receives financial support from ______.
5 The advantage of the technique being developed by Diels is that it can be used ______.
6 The main difficulty associated with using the laser equipment is related to its ______.
